# Introduction

## 0) Assignment Syntax

```{r}
# R code here
a <- 5 # traditional way of assignment
print(a)
```

## 1) Variables and Datatypes

### a) Four Basic Datatypes

```{r}
my_int = 2L # L to specify integer
my_double = 2.5 # double, or numeric
my_char = "Hi" # character
my_logical = TRUE # all caps TRUE or FALSE for logical

# check datatype with typeof

typeof(my_char)
typeof(my_double)
```

### b) Variable Names

- A variable name must start with a letter and can be a combination of letters, digits, period(.) and underscore(\_). If it starts with period(.), it cannot be followed by a digit.
- A variable name cannot start with a number or underscore (\_)
- Variable names are case-sensitive (age, Age and AGE are three different variables)
- Reserved words cannot be used as variables (TRUE, FALSE, NULL, if…)

## 2) Print and Input Statements

```{r}
print(paste("My character value is", my_char))
print(paste0("My character value is", my_char))
```

```{r}
# sprintf function takes placeholder %d, %s, %i, etc.
# %d and %f for numerics
# %s for characters

sprintf("My character value is %s and my integer is %d", my_char, my_int)
```

## 4) Built-in Functions

- The idea is the same as Python

- The syntax is the same: Function name, the inputs inside parantheses etc.

- A conceptual comparison between Python and R usage:

- Python is a general-purpose language:

  - Can be used for any task
  - The toolbox of functions in base Python is very limited
  - You import/install libraries for access to the functions

- R has stats/numeric operations as its main focus:

  - It has a way more extensive set of functions in base R.
  - Everything is implemented through functions.
  - R DOES NOT HAVE ANY METHODS AND ATTRIBUTES!
  - It still has many libraries for many different tasks, none will be used in this course.

## 5) Errors

- Same as Python, there are syntax, runtime, semantic errors.

## 6) Last Note

- RStudio is a more user-friendly environment than Jupyter.
- R functions avoid throwing errors as much as possible. That means you can encounter more semantic errors than you did in Python.
